raw_response.rationale: Qualitative ethnographic and interview-based study (26 interviews across 10 households in formal Litha Park and informal Endlovini in Khayelitsha plus 3 City of Cape Town water officials, alongside municipal policy analysis) examining how Cape Town's water governance and Day Zero drought response worsened intra-township water inequality. Multiple legal and administrative mechanisms operate co-equally: (1) fees_tariffs_subsidies (the municipal cost-recovery model, punitive one-size-fits-all water tariffs ignoring multi-household/backyarder yards, and limits of the 6 kL/month means-tested Free Basic Water policy, which anchors the paper's central thesis), (2) eligibility_status_documentation (municipal classification of settlements as formal vs unauthorized/illegal occupation to justify withholding planned services and maintenance), (3) enforcement_sanctions (installation of water management devices overriding indigent FBW protections and disproportionate drought water restrictions/unscheduled cutoffs), (4) participation_assistance (exclusion of informal settlement residents from community leadership and municipal consultative processes), and (5) review_redress (unequal access to municipal maintenance complaint channels tied to formal billing). Outcomes span effective_access (primary: severe supply restrictions below 25 L/person/day, unscheduled water cuts, shared broken/leaking communal standpipes serving ~50 people, and unmaintained burst pipes/sewers), economic_access (exorbitant bills, indigent households forced to pay for leak losses, and tariff pass-through to backyard tenants), and administrative_outcome (differential municipal responsiveness to logged maintenance complaints).
